Sweden joins NATO, ending decades of military nonalignment

WASHINGTON, March 7, 2024 — Sweden formally joined NATO on Thursday, becoming the alliance’s 32nd member after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine prompted a historic shift in its security policy.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken attended the accession ceremony in Washington, where Sweden deposited its instrument of accession with the U.S. government.

Sweden and Finland applied to join the alliance in May 2022. Finland became a member in April 2023, while Sweden’s application took longer to secure the unanimous approval required from existing allies. Turkey and Hungary were the last members to ratify Sweden’s entry.

Membership brings Sweden under NATO’s collective-defence commitment, which treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all. It also deepens the alliance’s military presence around the Baltic Sea.

The accession ends Sweden’s longstanding policy of military nonalignment, although the country had already cooperated closely with NATO through joint exercises and international operations.

Finland joins NATO in historic security shift

BRUSSELS, April 4, 2023 — Finland joined NATO on Tuesday, becoming the alliance’s 31st member and ending decades of military nonalignment following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finnish Foreign Minister Pekka Haavisto handed the country’s instrument of accession to U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken at NATO headquarters in Brussels, completing the formal entry process. Finland’s flag was then raised alongside those of the other allies.

Finland and Sweden applied for membership in May 2022, abandoning longstanding policies of staying outside the alliance. Finland’s accession followed ratification by all 30 existing members, with Turkey the last to approve its application.

The move brings Finland under NATO’s collective-defence commitment and roughly doubles the length of the alliance’s land border with Russia. Finland shares a border of about 1,340 kilometres with its eastern neighbour.

Sweden’s application remained pending, with Turkey and Hungary yet to ratify its membership. NATO decisions on admitting new countries require unanimous approval.

Russia opposed the alliance’s expansion. NATO described Finland’s entry as a step that would strengthen both Finnish security and the alliance’s collective defence.

Sweden joins NATO after historic shift in security policy

WASHINGTON, March 7, 2024 — Sweden formally joined NATO on Thursday, becoming the alliance’s 32nd member nearly two years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine prompted it to seek membership.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken attended a ceremony in Washington as Sweden deposited its instrument of accession with the U.S. government, completing the entry process.

Sweden and Finland applied to join NATO in May 2022, reversing longstanding policies of military nonalignment. Finland joined in April 2023, but Sweden faced a longer ratification process as Turkey and Hungary delayed approval.

NATO requires unanimous consent from its existing members to admit a new country. Hungary’s parliament approved Sweden’s bid on Feb. 26, clearing the final parliamentary obstacle.

Membership brings Sweden under NATO’s collective-defence framework. Article 5 of the alliance’s founding treaty treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all, with each ally taking such action as it considers necessary to assist.

Sweden’s accession also expands NATO’s presence around the Baltic Sea. The country already had close military ties with the alliance through joint exercises and operations, but membership gives it a formal role in collective defence planning.
